title: Levels of Consensus
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article introduces a practical tool for testing where a team actually stands on a decision, distinguishing consensus from unanimous agreement. It lays out six levels of conviction, ranging from enthusiastic championing of a decision down to a member needing to block it outright, and argues teams waste significant time re-litigating decisions where consensus already quietly exists. The author frames the tool as a quick way for leaders to gauge conviction levels before investing further discussion time, reserving deeper debate for the genuinely contested issues.
points: Consensus is defined as everyone being able to live with a decision, not full agreement.
A six-level scale of conviction, from enthusiastic support to blocking, helps teams quickly gauge where they stand.
Teams often waste time continuing to discuss decisions where consensus already exists.
The tool is meant to save discussion time for genuinely contested issues rather than settled ones.
quotes: Consensus is not agreement. Reaching consensus in a group means everyone can live with the decision or choice.
Too many teams continue to discuss decisions and issues where consensus already exists.
Levels of Consensus is one such device that is used widely in effective organizations.
Expressing a level is not a vote but a measure of conviction at a given point in time.
Using the Levels of Consensus tool to test where the group stands on an issue before a discussion can save valuable time.
